b: In this “Ask Me Anything” (AMA) episode, Peter explores what laboratory testing can—and cannot—tell us about our health. Blood tests provide objective numbers and reference ranges, making them an appealing way to assess overall health. But their usefulness is far more nuanced than it may appear. Peter begins by explaining how to interpret lab results in the context of both lifespan and healthspan, emphasizing the importance of tracking changes over time rather than relying on isolated measurements. He then examines the strengths and limitations of blood testing for assessing risk across the major chronic diseases, including cardiovascular disease, metabolic dysfunction, cancer, and neurodegenerative disease. He explains what labs can reveal about organ health and where additional information from imaging, body composition, and functional testing is needed. The conversation also explores why more testing does not necessarily lead to better clinical decisions. Peter discusses the limitations of large direct-to-consumer testing panels and sophisticated measures such as lipid subfractionation and biological-age scores, particularly when the results lack clear clinical actionability. He also highlights the importance of physical function, cognitive performance, and emotional health—critical components of healthspan that cannot be adequately captured through blood work alone. Finally, Peter provides a practical framework for evaluating any laboratory test, understanding its limitations, and determining whether the results offer meaningful information that can guide decisions about health and longevity.

What do patients hope to learn when they review their labs?

More broadly, there’s a belief that by the end of the exercise, the patient expects to know everything they need to know about their health
A subset of that is, “Am I healthy?”

It’s a very understandable assumption to come into a lab assessment with
Because, for the most part, when you’ve interacted with the health care system, the only routine maintenance things that tend to get done are lab testing

We tend to think of imaging in a separate category
Obviously, a woman who gets her mammogram every year would also consider that a part of her routine health maintenance
But for most people, when we interact with our doctors, we’re doing so around lab tests

Lab tests are: objective, numerical—they have these reverence ranges
All of these things about them make them feel like they should be complete

If nothing falls outside a reference range and nothing is flagged, people assume, “All systems are go”
The “check-engine light” isn’t coming on, so everything seems okay
And that view has probably been amplified over the past few years because there is really no shortage of direct-to-consumer testing products out there
Direct-to-consumer testing has doubled down on that belief system: lab tests are the thing you need to know
The promise is that if you buy a DTC product that checks many labs, it will have the solution to every problem
With patients, Peter starts by explaining where labs are valuable and where their blind spots are
Lab tests will show roughly 25% of what we care to know about you
And that’s a very important %, but we have a lot of work to do to really get under the hood of truly understanding risk across everything that we care about
